Room

Off, every wall is one band of the thickness above and the room size is to the structure. On, each wall is set out layer by layer — tile, adhesive, waterproofing, lining, frame — and Width and Length become the finished, tiled clear sizes, because the build-up is drawn outward from them. On the plan the wall keeps whatever poché it has — blank stays blank, and the build-up shows as the line between the lining and the frame, which is as much as 1:20 can carry. Set a poché pattern below to see the layers in their own colours.

User guide

Bathroom · sanitaryware and joinery drawing sets

Everything here is driven from one model of the job. Set the room out, stand fixtures in it, and the plans, elevations and schedules all follow. You do not draw twice. Every panel and control named in this guide is one you will find in the app — it is written from the app rather than about it.

1 · Where everything is

The window is in four bands.

  • The header, with undo and redo, save, export, fold panels and the library.
  • The tab strip, which is the drawing set. Each tab is a sheet, numbered in the order it prints and grouped: cover and summary, plans, elevations, schedules. Site measure and this guide sit at the two ends and carry no number, because they are working tabs rather than sheets.
  • The sidebars, left and right, holding the panels. Drag a panel's → or ← arrow to move it from one side to the other.
  • The sheet itself, with the zoom controls at the right of the tab strip and a line at the bottom left telling you what you can do on this sheet.

How the job nests

Knowing the order explains most of the app:

Project → job → rooms → walls → rows → fixtures

  • A project is a client or an address, and holds jobs.
  • A job is one drawing set — one bathroom, one PDF.
  • A job has one or more rooms, each bringing its own walls and elevation sheets into the same set.
  • Each wall is lettered and gets an elevation.
  • Each wall has two rows: the base row stands on the floor, the wall row hangs.
  • A row is a run, laid out left to right, with fillers, panels and gaps between the fixtures.
Worth knowing. Settings nest the same way. A job-wide default applies everywhere until a wall or a single fixture is given its own, and that override wins for that one thing. It is why a job default can look ignored — something below it has been set by hand. Inherit project default hands it back.

2 · Getting around

Doing thisGets you
ScrollZoom in and out on the sheet
Shift-dragPan the sheet
− Fit +The same, from the right of the tab strip. Fit puts the whole sheet back on screen.
[ ]Previous and next sheet
Click a fixtureSelects it and turns the sidebar into its edit panel
EscLets go of it

A tab shown faintly is one switched off in Sheets to issue. It still opens and still draws; it just will not print.

⌃ Fold panels in the header collapses every panel at once, for when you want the drawing and nothing else. Press it again to open them.

3 · Starting a job

Project holds the project name, job name, client, who drew it, and a logo. All of it prints in the title block, so it is worth filling in before you issue.

The library

Library in the header lists every project and the jobs inside it.

＋ New projectStart a fresh project.
Save current as new job…Branch what is on screen into a new job — how you draw an option B without losing option A.
Import JSONBring in a job someone has sent you.

Saving

The job autosaves as you work. Ctrl+S or Save writes it now and marks a point undo can come back to. Export writes the current job to a JSON file — that file is the whole job, so it is what you send someone or keep as a backup.

Reset to demo at the bottom right throws away what is on screen and starts from the sample job. It does not touch the library, and Ctrl+Z will undo it.

4 · The room

Room sets the shell.

Width · Length · CeilingThe room in plan, and how high the elevations run.
Wall thicknessHow thick the walls are cut on the plan, and what a niche has to fit inside.
NorthThe north point on the plan.
Wall materialPlasterboard, timber or steel stud, brick veneer, double brick, single skin, blockwork, Hebel, in-situ or precast concrete, stone, rammed earth, or no wall shown. It decides the colour and the poché pattern the walls are cut in.
Poché patternOverrides the pattern the material would use.

Walls are lettered clockwise and each gets an elevation. Rooms adds further rooms to the same job. Openings puts doors and windows into a chosen wall; they are drawn on the plan and on that wall's elevation, and a door shows its swing.

5 · Site measure

The Site measure tab is a tracing surface, not a sheet. Trace the room on it, then press Bring in from Draw — on that tab or in the Site measure panel — and the outline becomes the room, with one elevation per wall however many walls it has and whatever shape it is.

⤢ ExpandGives the tracing the whole window. Esc brings the tabs back.
Import file…Takes a measure done elsewhere.
Re-letter around the planRenames the walls in order once the shape is right.
Back to a rectangleAbandons a traced outline for a plain rectangular room.

6 · Walls, runs and rows

Fixtures & joinery is where a wall is built up. The Room and Active wall pill bars at the top decide what the rest of that panel — and the whole Run trim (active wall) panel — are talking about. Change the active wall and both change with it.

Below them are the two rows, each with its own list and its own ＋ to add. The list is the run in order.

Run fit

The readout under the wall pills adds up what is on the wall against the wall's length, so you can see at a glance whether the run fits and by how much it is over or under.

Elevation shows

An elevation normally draws the whole wall. Elevation shows crops it to a stretch — type the two numbers, or drag the break line on the sheet itself. whole wall puts it back. Use it when a wall is long and the detail being issued is at one end.

7 · Putting fixtures in

Pick the room and wall, choose the type from the dropdown on the row you want, and press ＋. It goes on the end of that run; move it from there.

GroupWhat you can add
SanitarywareToilet suite · Shower · Bath · Basin — wall hung / pedestal · Blade wall
VanitiesVanity — basin + tap · Vanity — drawers · Vanity — door + shelves · Corner — vanity (blind L)
Tall and wallLinen tower / tallboy · Shaving / wall cabinet · Corner — wall (blind L)
Hung on the wallMirror · Towel rail · Niche
LaundryLaundry tub + tap · Washer / dryer — under bench · Dryer — wall mounted
FillersVanity 720 high · Tall 2100 high · Wall 750 high

A Freestanding vanity is not on a wall, so it has its own panel rather than a place in a run: centre X and Y, length, depth, angle, stool overhang, and its own top material, stone hatch and thickness. It gets its own elevation sheet.

8 · Editing one fixture

Click a fixture on any sheet, or its name in the list, and the sidebar becomes its edit panel. Esc lets go; Del removes it. The panel is always in the same order, so it can be learnt once.

SectionWhat is in it
DimensionsWidth, height, depth.
MountingOn a kick or wall hung, with a kick height for this unit only. The job default is in Carcass.
Group withTies fixtures together so they are dimensioned and read as one item.
Its own typeThe section named for what it is — Sink, Screen, Tray and outlet, Blade wall. Covered one by one below.
HandleStyle and finish for this unit, overriding the project default. Not offered on sanitaryware, which has no handles.
Blum hardwareRunner and hinge specification for this unit.
DimensionLock dim value prints a number you type instead of the real width, for when the drawing must call out a site dimension. Note appended to dim text adds your words after it.
Adjacent fillers & panelsLeft and right filler and panel widths — see the next section.
SettingsLabel on the drawing, and the resets: return the basin, the tap or the hardware to defaults.
ActionsCopy settings and Paste onto this one to make a second fixture match the first, and Delete cabinet.

Some sidebar panels rename themselves for what is selected. Select a blade wall and Finish (fronts) becomes Top of blade, and its swatches colour that blade's top rather than the job's fronts.

9 · Position along a wall

Every fixture stands at its own set-out, measured from the start of the run to its near edge. Moving one moves that one; everything else on the wall stays where it is. Two ways, and they do the same thing:

  • Drag the fixture along the plan or its elevation. Dropped near the edge of another fixture, the run start or the end of the wall, it goes hard against it; dropped anywhere else it stays exactly where you let go.
  • Type the figure into Set-out from start of run in its own panel, under Position along the wall. A typed figure is taken as given and is not snapped.

The list order follows the wall: move a fixture past another and the two change places in the list, because that is now the order they stand in.

Nothing is ever pushed out of the way. Two things cannot stand in the same place, so a fixture dropped on top of another goes alongside it instead — whichever side is nearer. Take it well past and it goes where you took it, stepping over what it passed rather than shoving it along the wall. The fixture in your hand is the only one that moves, and that holds however tightly the wall is packed.

Height counts. Two wall fixtures are only in each other's way if they share a band of height as well as a stretch of wall. A roll holder at 700 and a shaving cabinet at 1420 never touch, so the roll holder hangs under the cabinet and neither is placed with any regard to the other. Two cabinets at the same height still keep out of each other's way, and so does everything standing on the floor — joinery cannot be made to interpenetrate.

Nothing travels with anything unless you have grouped it. Group two fixtures and they move together, keeping the spacing between them; that is what a group is for, and it is the only thing that does it.

Left filler, Left panel, Right filler and Right panel in the same panel say what fills the space beside a fixture, not where that fixture stands. A panel is an end panel, and a filler is a strip of board across the gap in front — so the gap is the figure, and the filler is how it is drawn. Move either fixture and the gap between them changes, which means the filler across it changes with it.

Run trim (active wall) holds what belongs to the run rather than to one unit: left and right scribe fillers, end-panel thickness, the wall's own tile, the low wall, and the bench — whether it runs on this wall at all, and how far past each end.

10 · Vanity — basin + tap

The most-used fixture in the app, and the one with the most in it. Under Sink:

BowlsSingle, 1.5 or double, with bowl width and bowl depth.
Bowl shapeOval, round, soft-cornered rectangle, or rectangle. Plan and elevation both follow it. A round bowl takes the smaller of width and depth, so it stays round whatever you set.
Basin mountUndermount, drop-in, or on top — see below.
Basin height above benchOffered only for a basin on top.
Sink offsetSlides the bowls along the cabinet without moving the cabinet.
Tap mountOn the bench, or a wall mixer.
Wall tap above benchHeight for a wall mixer, measured off the benchtop. Wall taps only.
Tap styleBasin, standard, gooseneck, tall, tall gooseneck. Bench taps only.
Tap positionBehind the bowl, or clear of it left or right.

Basin mount, and why it matters

This is not a drawing preference — it is what the benchtop is fabricated to. An undermount cut-out is polished on its edge because you can see it and run your hand over it; a drop-in is not, because the rim covers it; a basin standing on top needs nothing cut but a hole for the waste.

So the drawing says which. On the plan an undermount bowl is dashed because it is work under the top, a drop-in shows its rim lapping the bench, and one on top is drawn solid and a line weight heavier because it is an object standing in the room. On the elevation an undermount bowl stays hidden detail under the top, a drop-in shows its rim proud of the bench, and one on top stands on the bench in china. The waste follows: from the bottom of the bowl where one hangs under the bench, from the underside of the top where it does not.

Tapware

The tap is drawn behind the basin on the elevation, so a basin standing on the bench laps over the foot of its tap and what shows above the rim is the spout — which is all you would see standing in the room.

Worth knowing. A basin mixer is a shorter thing than a kitchen tap, and a basin standing on the bench needs one taller than either. A 150 riser behind a 130 vessel is a tap pouring down its side. That is what Tall and Tall goose are for.

The rest of the cabinet

Below the sink section: False front — the dummy drawer over the bowl and its height; Shelves, with a bowl clearance so a shelf is never drawn through the basin; Below sink — doors or drawers, how many, hinge side; and Front style.

The same family without a cabinet under it.

Bowl shapeThe same four shapes as the vanity.

Wall tap above rimWall mixers only. Measured off the rim rather than the floor, because that is what you choose it against — so it follows the basin when the rim height changes.

13 · Shower

The busiest fixture, in two sections.

Screen

ConfigurationWalk-in with no screen · fixed panel · fixed panel + hinged door · hinged door only · pivot door · sliding, two panels · fixed panel + return · corner, return + hinged door.
Fixed panel atWhich side the fixed panel stands.
Hinge sideWhich side the door hangs from.
SwingOut into the room, or back into the tray. The door and its arc are drawn on the plan either way.
Clear openingThe opening you actually walk through.
Return panelWidth of the return, where the configuration has one.
Side wallNone, or a tiled blade wall. It replaces the glass on the side it stands on.
Blade on · thickness · projection · heightWhich side, how thick, how far it reaches (0 = the full depth of the tray) and how high.
FramingHow the glass is held.
Hardware finishMatt black · brushed brass · brushed nickel · chrome · frameless, no hardware colour. It shows as the colour of the glass edge.
Glass thicknessDrawn to scale, so a 10 reads differently from a 6.
Screen heightHow high the glass runs.

Tray and outlet

BaseTiled, or a manufactured tray. A tiled base is floor, so the floor tiling runs through it on the plan rather than being hidden — which is the one place the set-out is most often argued about.
Waste · positionLinear or square, and where it sits: centre, left, right, inside against the wall or outside at the entry. A linear waste laid across the shower runs the width; one down a side turns with it. The falls are drawn from each corner to wherever the waste actually is, dashed, the way a waterproofer reads them.
Hob height · widthA kerb across the front. It is outlined rather than filled, so the tiling still reads through it.
Mixer wallThe back wall, or either return. A mixer on the return is what you put in when you do not want to reach through the water to turn it on. On the return the fitting turns with the wall, and on the elevation it is dashed, because it is on a wall at right angles to that sheet.
Mixer positionUnder the head, or any of the same five the waste and outlet use. On the back wall left, right and centre place it across; on a return inside and outside place it in depth. A set-out typed into Mixer across still wins, and is only offered for the back wall.
Mixer heightHow high it sits. It is drawn on the plan as well as the elevation, because it is a set-out a plumber works to.
OutletRainhead on a wall arm · rainhead from the ceiling · rail shower, handheld · rail + rainhead, twin outlet · rail + ceiling rainhead.
Outlet positionThe same five: centre, left, right, inside or outside. Left, right and centre move it across the shower; inside and outside move it in depth, which a rail on the wall has no use for and ignores.
Rainhead shape · size · height · out from wallRound or square, and where it sits. A ceiling rose is dashed on the plan, the way anything overhead is.
Arm reachHow far the arm comes off the wall.
Rail topTop of the rail, for a rail shower.

14 · Toilet

Suite typeBack to wall · back to wall with a concealed cistern · close coupled · wall hung. The two concealed ones put the cistern in the wall and give you a flush plate; the difference between them is that a back-to-wall pan still stands on the floor and a wall-hung one does not.
TrapP or S trap — which decides where the waste goes, and is the thing worth getting right before the slab is poured.
Set-outWall to pan centre. The number the plumber works to.
Pan width · projectionThe pan itself.
Seat heightTo the top of the seat.
Cistern / top heightTop of an exposed cistern. Not offered on a concealed one, which has no top of its own.
Flush plate heightConcealed cisterns only. The cistern is drawn around the plate rather than at a height of its own, because the plate is what it is set out from on site.
Pan height off floorWall hung only. The gap under the pan, which is the thing people actually decide, because it is what gets cleaned under.

15 · Mirror, rail and niche

These go in the wall row, so they draw over whatever is below them.

MirrorWidth and height from Dimensions, Bottom above floor, and an Edge treatment.
Towel railHeight above floor and the number of Rails, so a single, a double and a ladder are all drawn properly — on the plan as well, which used to show one tube however many were ordered.
Toilet roll holderThe open sort: a round plate, a short elbow and a bar running along the wall with a cap on the end. Height above floor, the length of the bar, and which hand it is — the bar runs away from the plate, and which way decides whether it reaches over the pan or over the wall beside it. The roll itself is not drawn; it is the fitting being specified.
Hand towel holderA ring or a short bar, at a height.
Towel hookOne to four hooks on a plate, at a height.
Soap dishSmall for a bar or large for a bottle, at a height. The two are different products rather than one scaled, so they are drawn at their own sizes — 130 across for the small and 190 for the large.
Shower shelfA shelf on two plates, at a height, with a front lip you can turn off.
NicheBottom above floor and Shelves.
Worth knowing. A niche is formed inside the wall, so its panel tells you how much depth the wall actually leaves once it is lined, and warns you when you ask for more. It is the difference between a niche and a hole through to the next room. A low wall in front changes that answer.

16 · Cabinets and fillers

Vanity — drawersDrawer count and how the heights are split, equal or set by hand.
Vanity — door + shelvesDoor count, hinge side, shelves.
Linen tower / tallboyDoors and shelves, plus Side panels — end panels outside the carcass, to the floor or to the ceiling, at a thickness you set.
Shaving / wall cabinetThe wall row equivalent, with doors and shelves, and a bottom height above FFL of its own. Left alone it follows the bench and splashback.
Corner vanity · corner wallBlind L corners, with the blind return set so the door and the return do not fight.
FillersVanity, tall and wall height. A filler beside a tall unit is a vertical scribe running the full height of that cabinet, so the benchtop stops at the base run rather than running over it.
Laundry tub + tapA sink cabinet with a deep single bowl; it shares the sink controls and the tapware.
Washer / dryerMachine type, freestanding or integrated, and whether the bench runs over it.

A few sections in the edit panel — Rangehood, Pelmets, Fridge — are inherited from the joinery app this one grew out of. They appear on the cabinet types that can carry them and do no harm on a bathroom job.

17 · Blade and low walls

Both are built work rather than joinery, and the app treats them alike.

Low wall

In Run trim (active wall): a stud wall built off the wall behind it, with a height, a thickness, where it starts and stops, a capping across the top and its own tile, colour and grout.

Worth knowing. Anything starting below the low wall's top fixes to it and comes forward by its thickness; anything at or above its top goes on the wall behind. So a niche placed low sits in the low wall, and the same niche placed high sits in the wall behind it.

Blade wall

A fixture in the base row: a built, tiled wall running out from the wall into the room. Its width is its thickness and its depth is how far it reaches. Tile sets what it is finished in, or leave it on (same as the wall).

A shower can also carry a blade as its side wall, set in the shower's own Screen section rather than added separately. It is drawn whether or not there is any glass beside it, because a built wall stands there either way.

How both are drawn

On a plan both are cut in the same colour the room's own walls are cut in, and follow the wall material with them — a plan already carries the floor, the walls and the joinery, and another flat tone in it makes a built wall read as furniture. On an elevation both show their tiling, because that is the view where you are looking at tiling.

A blade can be given a colour of its own: select it, and the swatch panel renames itself Top of blade and colours that blade. A reset beside the colour picker puts it back to matching the walls.

18 · Finishes

PanelWhat it sets
Finish (fronts)Colour and door style for every front on the job — slab, shaker, V-groove, fluted, glass in a frame, mirror in a frame. One cabinet can differ in its own panel.
CarcassBoard thickness, kick height, filler depth.
Vanity topMaterial, height, front overhang, top thickness, edge profile, brand and product name, surface finish, and the hatch it is drawn in. Engineered stone, porcelain and sintered stone, natural stone, terrazzo, solid surface, timber, laminate, concrete and a tiled top, each at the thickness it is made in — and a thickness of your own where the same material comes more than one way. Choosing an engineered stone raises a note in the panel: it has been banned in Australia for new benchtops since 1 July 2024 and is legal for documenting or repairing an existing installation.
Wall tilingThe job's tile: type, brand, product, size, bond and laying pattern, tiling height, the height the tiling starts at — which may be below FFL, so a floor laid to falls is set out off its lowest point — and which end the part course goes. Mosaics through subway and squares to 1200 × 2400 slab.
Tile on this wallIn Run trim: one wall's tile, colour and grout. Leave it on the job's tile and the wall follows the project; set it and only that wall changes.
FloorMaterial and laying pattern — boards, herringbone, chevron, parquet, planks, tiles from 100 × 100 to slab — the size, the angle it is laid at, and where the set-out starts, nudged across and along until the cuts fall where you want them.
Finishes boardMaterials, colours and photographs of samples, kept in the job and printed with it. Photographs are scaled down on the way in, so a phone photo does not make the job file unusable.
Worth knowing. Setting a wall's tile makes that wall tiled. The finish type — tiled, painted, rendered — is job-wide, so one wall painted and the rest tiled is not something the app can draw yet.

19 · Electrical, lighting and wastes

Electrical & lighting sets the brand and plate finish, a default mounting height, and the tag position on elevations. Press Place, then click where it goes on an elevation or the plan. Esc cancels placing.

Power and switchesSingle, double, vertical double, quad, double + USB, floor box, IP rated; 1 to 4 gang switches, dimmers, appliance isolators, data points.
Cabinet lightingLED strip under a wall cabinet, in a shadowline, in the plinth, on a shelf, over a cabinet as an uplight, in a handleless rail, washing the toe kick; puck downlights, spotlights, door sensor switches, driver locations.
Room lightingDownlights, fixed or gimbal, and pendants, with a colour temperature.

A fitting inside a cabinet is drawn as hidden detail, because that is what it is — a strip on a shelf is behind a door just as much as a socket is. Click one to select it and Del to remove it. Floor wastes are placed the same way from the Floor panel.

Measure is a tape: press Start measuring and click two points on a sheet. The tape follows the cursor between the two clicks with the figure running on it, catches on the corners and faces of anything on the sheet, and squares itself up when it is within a couple of degrees of square — so a measurement off a cabinet face is the face, not near it. It is drawn the way the sheet's own dimensions are, in red, and it stays on the sheet it was taken on. Esc drops a half-made one and again puts the tape away; clicking a figure asks whether to keep that measurement or delete it, Clear removes them all from the sheet, and Ctrl+Z takes any of it back.

A measurement already on the sheet is dragged rather than retaken. Take hold of either end to correct it — the end catches and squares up as it would if it were being placed for the first time — or take hold of the line to move the whole thing off whatever it is sitting over. The cursor says which it will be. The whole drag is one undo step.

The tape's colour, line weight and figure size are set in the same panel, along with the box behind the figure — its shape (rectangle, rounded, pill, ellipse, or no outline) and what is behind it (opaque white, opaque colour with the figure reversed out, or clear). An opaque tag reads over anything on the sheet; clear is the lightest and will not read over a tile hatch. They are one setting for the job rather than per measurement: a sheet of measurements in four colours reads as a mess rather than as a key. The colour is deliberately not the drawing's own ink, so a measurement is never mistaken for something the sheet is asserting. The settings are saved with the job.

An elevation shows what returns into it from the walls either side. A bath on wall B is right there at the end of the view when you look at wall A, so it is drawn there: seen end on, as wide as it is deep, dashed because it is beyond the plane of the elevation rather than on it. This wall's own joinery goes down after it and stands in front, which is the truth of what you would see. Only what reaches the shared corner is drawn — everything in the room projects onto an elevation if you are strict about it, and an elevation drawn strictly that way is a stack of outlines nobody can read. Turn it off under Drawing style.

The tiling shows on the floor plans as well: a band on each wall face with the perpends ticked across it, running the same set-out the elevations do and stopping either side of every door and window. It is a notation rather than a measured layer — ten millimetres of tile and bed is finer than a hairline at 1:50, so the band is drawn at its real thickness where that reads and at a fixed depth on the page where it does not. The joints are the point of it. Turn it off in Wall tiling where the plan is busy enough already.

Underneath is every measurement in the job, listed under the sheet it was taken on, with its figure. Pointing at a row lights that measurement up on the drawing; clicking one goes to its sheet; the cross on the row deletes that one. Which is the way to pick three measurements out of a dozen spread over a plan and two elevations — Clear takes a whole sheet's worth, and hunting for the right figure to click is the slow way round.

Callouts is a note with a leader — the way a drawing says what a thing is rather than how big it is. Press Add a callout and click what it points at; the note lands clear of it and you type it there, Enter for a second line. Drag its head to move what it points at, or its note to move the note; click the note to edit it again — clicking anywhere on it, note, head or leader, opens the note. It is drawn in the sheet's own dimension style — same ink, same weight, same text size — because a note that does not match the dimensions beside it reads as something stuck on afterwards. The leader head (arrow, dot or nothing), the shoulder line under the note, the box behind it and the colour are all set in the panel, and the colour's reset puts it back to following the sheet. Callouts are listed by sheet the same way measurements are.

20 · Handles and hardware

Project handle default sets the handle for the job: none / push-to-open, shark nose / finger pull, J-pull edge profile, knob, D-pull, bar pull, or recessed slot — with its finish, and the finger gap and rail dimensions where the style uses them. Any cabinet can carry a different one in its own panel, and Inherit project default hands it back.

Blum hardware records the specification the job is built to: system, drawer side height, load class, motion, colour, hinge family, opening angle, application and special application, cup fixing, and AVENTOS lift systems. It is what gets ordered, so it belongs on the drawing rather than in someone's head. A single cabinet can differ in its own panel.

21 · Dimensions and drawing style

Drawing style controls how the set looks rather than what is in it: object line weight and colour, dimension line weight and colour, dimension text size, and the angle door swings are drawn at.

The dim note fields — kick, cabinet face, bench thickness, bench height, splashback, room height — append your own words to those dimensions, so a set can carry your office's wording without editing each sheet.

On a single fixture, Lock dim value prints a number you type instead of its real width, and Note appended to dim text adds words after it.

Panel headings sizes and colours each sidebar heading on its own — the point being to tell one group of panels from another at a glance. Reset all to default undoes the lot.

22 · Schedules and issuing

Sheets to issue lists every sheet with a switch. Turn one off and it drops out of the PDF and out of the cover index, and its tab goes faint. All on and All off do the lot.

Download drawing set (PDF) at the bottom right writes every issued sheet in order, at A3 landscape.

The cover, the summary and both schedules are generated from the job. If something reads wrong on a schedule it is wrong in the drawing — fix it there and the schedule follows.

Keyboard reference

ScrollZoom
Shift-dragPan
ClickSelect a fixture and open its panel
DragMove a fixture along its wall
[ ]Previous · next sheet
EscDeselect · cancel placing · close the library · leave full-window tracing · stop measuring
Del BackspaceDelete the selected fixture or fitting

Inside a text field, Ctrl+Z undoes your typing rather than the drawing.

What is on each sheet

SheetWhat it carries
CoverTitle block, project details, and an index of the sheets being issued.
Project summaryThe room, the finishes and the specification on one page.
Floor plan — fixturesThe plan without wall cupboards, so the floor set-out reads. The accessories — rails, roll holder, hooks, dish, shelf — stay on it, because they are fixtures and belong beside what they serve.
Floor plan — with wall units & mirrorsThe same plan with everything that hangs shown over it.
ElevationsOne per wall, per room, plus the freestanding vanity where there is one.
Fixture scheduleEvery cabinet with its sizes and settings.
Sanitaryware scheduleFixtures and tapware with brands, models and cut-outs.
Site measure · User guideWorking tabs. No sheet number, never issued, not in the PDF.

If it looks wrong

What you seeWhat it is
No benchtopBench enabled is per wall, in Run trim (active wall). Check the active wall is the one the vanity is on.
Moving one fixture moved anotherA wall is a run, so everything after the one you moved shifts with it. Take the space back off the next fixture's left filler.
A sheet will not printIts switch is off in Sheets to issue — its tab will be faint.
A niche is too deepThe panel says how much the wall leaves once lined. A low wall in front changes that answer.
A setting has no effectAn override on the fixture beats the job default, so the default looks ignored until you reset it.
One wall's tile will not changeThe job-wide tile is in Wall tiling; one wall is Tile on this wall in Run trim, and it only affects the active wall.

4 · Your data and privacy

The software runs entirely on your own device. Projects, drawings, site measures, photos, logos, colour palettes and samples are stored locally — in this application's own storage and in the project files you save. There is no account, no server, and no usage tracking or telemetry: your project data is not transmitted to Draw Spec or to any third party.

One exception, and only where you use it: the Ask Claude panel sends what you type — and the drawing, if you hand one over — to Anthropic's Claude service through the Claude Code tool installed on your own machine, under your own Anthropic account and their terms. Nothing is sent unless you ask. Leave the panel alone and nothing leaves the device.

Dictation is the other one, and it depends which of Windows' two speech engines is running. The older desktop engine recognises entirely on this machine and no audio leaves it. The modern engine — the one behind Win+H, and much the better of the two — requires Windows' speech privacy policy to be accepted, and Windows may then use its own online service to do the recognising, which means audio can be sent to Microsoft under their terms rather than ours. The panel says which engine it is using. If you have not turned that setting on in Windows, the older engine is what runs and nothing is sent anywhere.

Because the data is local, backups are your responsibility. Use Export to write a project file out, and keep copies of anything you would not want to lose. Clearing the application's storage, or uninstalling without exporting, will remove saved projects.
